newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns of penalties in Japan port dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns of penalties in Japan port dispute.

text.p: The United States warned on Monday that it will impose penalties on Japanese carriers if Tokyo does not move quickly to open access to its ports.

"Absent the comprehensive solution that we are seeking, the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission will impose fees of $100,000 per voyage on Japanese liner carriers calling at U.S. ports," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

The penalities, announced by the commission in February, are due to take effect on April 14. Burns spoke as U.S. and Japanese negotiators continued talks in Washington aimed at defusing the row. The talks began April 2.

He said Washington hoped the penalties would not have to be imposed. But for that to happen, he said, "the government of Japan needs to take prompt action to reform the prior consultative system and to open to foreign firms the licensing of stevedores and terminal operations in Japanese ports.

"Right now there isn't fair play. Other firms don't have access to the bidding on contracts that they should have," Burns said. He added that "costs in Japanese ports are among the highest anywhere in the world and they directly drive up the cost of both Japanese exports and Japanese imports."
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright raised the port issue with Japanese officials when she visited Tokyo in February and Vice President Al Gore discussed it during his recent trip to Japan.

Just two weeks ago, Albright visited the North Carolina headquarters of Sea-land Corp., the U.S. shipping giant that has been pushing hard to end Japanese port restrictions. Company officials said then that they had been pressing for reforms in this area for five years without success.
The company wants to be able to bring to Japan its own stevedores and terminal operations in an effort to lower costs and improve productivity, officials said.

At his news briefing on Monday, Burns said opening access to Japanese ports would be in line with other steps toward deregulation taken recently by Tokyo and would benefit Japanese as well as American consumers by lowering prices.
